name: Glycolic acid peel
lead: A glycolic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using glycolic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA). It is used to make skin look smoother, brighter and more even: Wikipedia describes AHA peels as the mildest peels, used for fine wrinkles, dryness, uneven pigment and acne, and one study article calls glycolic acid one of the most versatile agents in melasma treatment.[11][2]

The acid loosens the bonds between dead surface skin cells so the top layer sheds, revealing fresher skin and reducing visible pigment and texture irregularities. Professional peels use higher concentrations applied in an office, and lower-strength versions are sold for home use.[11][13] Studies in Indian and other patient groups have examined glycolic peels, at concentrations such as 20%, 30%, 35% or 70%, for melasma, periorbital melanosis and acne scars, alone, against other peels, or combined with other treatments.[1][2][3][4][8]
Glycolic acid occurs naturally in sugarcane, sugar beets, pineapple, cantaloupe and unripe grapes, and was named by Auguste Laurent in 1848.[13]

paras: Chemical peels remove the outermost skin layers by causing a controlled injury that makes the skin peel, usually on the face, and they are grouped by depth: light (AHA and BHA), medium (trichloroacetic acid) and deep (phenol-croton oil).[11] Glycolic acid is the best-known AHA peel agent; salicylic acid is the beta-hydroxy counterpart used for oilier, acne-prone skin.[11] Medium-depth peels are done by a medical provider, while light peels are the entry point.[11]
Glycolic acid is a small molecule with a pKa of 3.83 that dissolves readily in water; it is also described as a keratolytic agent used in acne treatment.[13]

Chemical peeling has a long history. In the 19th century the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra used agents such as phenol, croton oil and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities, phenol-croton oil peels were used quietly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s, and they entered mainstream practice in the 1960s through Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon.[11] Light alpha-hydroxy acid peels are a more recent, gentler development of the same idea.[11] Glycolic acid itself was first prepared by Adolph Strecker and Nikolai Sokolov in 1851.[13]

Glycolic acid peels are among the agents studied for melasma, a pigment disorder with brown patches on the face, either alone or with topical lightening agents.[2][5][9] They have also been studied for periorbital melanosis, the dark circles around the eyes, and for acne-related pigmentation.[1][3]

For acne scars, glycolic peels have been combined with microneedling in people with darker skin, where scars often coexist with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[1] Light peels are also used for dryness and fine texture.[11]

Glycolic acid is the smallest of the alpha hydroxy acids used in cosmetics, a family known for chemically exfoliating the skin; Wikipedia cites a 1994 supplement titled Alpha Hydroxy Acids for Skin Care and several peel and cream studies, including a 1999 report by Atzori and colleagues on glycolic peeling for acne and a 2001 study by Kalla and colleagues comparing glycolic and trichloroacetic acid peels for melasma.[15]

Concentration and pH matter for how these products behave. Expert panels at the FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review consider AHAs safe in products sold at low concentrations and a pH above 3.5 with thorough safety instructions, a framework that separates consumer products from the higher-strength peels given by providers.[15] The FDA has also warned consumers that AHAs can increase sun sensitivity and the likelihood of sunburn, an effect described as reversible after use stops, while other sources suggest glycolic acid may protect against some sun damage.[15] Product labels commonly advise daily sunscreen during use.
Glycolic acid is described as a keratolytic agent, meaning it loosens and sheds the outer layer of skin, which is the basis for its use in peels for pigment, texture and acne.[11][13]

A 2011 study combined microneedling with 35% glycolic acid peels for acne scars in dark skin: sixty patients were split between microneedling alone and microneedling with peels, and the combination group showed significant improvement in superficial and moderately deep scars, skin texture and post-acne pigmentation.[1]

A 2017 study of sixty patients with epidermal melasma compared serial glycolic peels every three weeks plus 20% azelaic acid cream against the cream alone over 24 weeks; improvement in the melasma severity index was significantly greater in the peel group from week 12, with greater gains in melasma quality-of-life scores and only minor reversible side effects.[2]

A comparative study of 90 patients with periorbital melanosis tested 20% glycolic peels, 15% lactic peels and 20% vitamin C over 12 weeks: more than 50% improvement occurred in about 73% of glycolic peel patients, 57% of lactic peel patients and 27% of vitamin C patients, and a later study added a 12% ferulic acid peel.[3][4]

Registered trials include glycolic acid against salicylic acid for melasma,[5][6] 70% glycolic acid with vitamin C for photoaging and acne scars,[7][8] and a comparison against a 1064 nm Q-switched laser for melasma.[9] A 2025 systematic review of randomized trials covered topical treatments for acanthosis nigricans.[10]

Wikipedia notes that complications rise with peel depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin thinning and photosensitivity, and that light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. It adds that both professional peels and low-strength home kits carry risks of injury and scarring.[11] Glycolic acid in concentrated form is classed as corrosive and a skin irritant in chemical safety data.[13]

In the periorbital melanosis comparison, adverse effects were most frequent with the glycolic peel, followed by the lactic peel and vitamin C.[3] In the melasma trial combining glycolic peels with azelaic acid, minor reversible side effects occurred in both groups and did not require stopping therapy.[2]

Peels sit within a broader cosmetic-dermatology market for brightening and smoothing treatments, and appear in beginner skincare conversation on forums such as T Nation, where members discuss facial care routines.[14] Light peels are provided by dermatologists and licensed estheticians, and lower-strength versions are sold for home use.[11]

card.summary: The most widely studied AHA peel, tested in melasma, periorbital darkening and acne scars in mostly small studies.
card.note: Stinging, redness and dryness are common; home kits have been associated with injury.

quick.overview:
A glycolic acid peel exfoliates the skin using an alpha-hydroxy acid and is used for pigmentation, acne scars and general texture.

It has the largest body of small comparative studies among the common peels, though many are from single centers.
quick.mechanism: It is a mild superficial peel that loosens the outer skin layers, which then shed.
quick.risks: Common effects are stinging, redness, irritation and dryness; pigment change is among reported complications, and Wikipedia notes weak home kits can cause injury and scarring.

chain: Glycolic acid applied to the face for a short period
Loosens and sheds the surface layer of dead skin cells
Smoother texture and more even tone, with fewer visible dark patches or mild scars
angle.text: People use glycolic peels, usually in a series spaced weeks apart, to brighten skin, soften fine texture and fade pigment such as melasma or post-acne marks. Results build over several sessions, and trials generally pair peels with sun protection or other topical treatments.
